# Commit message instructions

These are the rules for every commit message in this repository, including the
ones generated from the Source Control panel. They are checked in deliberately,
so that a message written by hand and a message generated by the editor read the
same way.

## Authorship

Write in the voice of the repository's author, as if they made the change
themselves — because they did; the tooling is an instrument, not a collaborator.

- **Never** add a `Co-Authored-By` trailer for an AI, assistant, model or tool.
- **Never** add "Generated with …", a robot emoji, or any other attribution line.
- **Never** name Copilot, Claude, ChatGPT or any other tool in the message.

If none of the change can be described without naming the tool that produced it,
describe the change instead.

## Shape

```
<subject: imperative, ≤ 72 characters, no full stop>

<body: wrapped at 72 columns>

<optional trailers: Fixes #123, Refs #456>
```

- Subject in the **imperative mood** — "Fix the paste-back seam on rotated
  frames", not "Fixed" or "Fixes" or "Fixing".
- Capitalise the subject; do not end it with a full stop.
- One blank line between subject and body, always.
- No Conventional Commits prefixes (`feat:`, `fix:`, `chore:`). This repository
  does not use them, and a machine-readable prefix is not a substitute for a
  sentence that says what happened.

## The body is the point

Be comprehensive and specific. A commit message is read years later by someone
trying to understand why the code is the way it is, usually while something is
broken. Assume they can already see the diff — what they cannot see is
everything that was in your head when you wrote it.

Always cover:

1. **What changed**, concretely. Name the types, functions and files that
   matter. "Refactored the engine" says nothing; "Moved the enhancer's session
   into a replica pool so two frames can be restored at once" says it.
2. **Why it changed.** The problem, the bug report, the measurement, the review
   comment. This is the part nobody can reconstruct later and the part most
   often left out.
3. **How it works**, when the approach is not obvious from the diff — the
   algorithm, the invariant it maintains, the ordering that matters.
4. **What was rejected and why**, when a simpler-looking approach exists and
   does not work. This is what stops the next person "simplifying" it back.
5. **Consequences**: behaviour changes, performance numbers with the conditions
   they were measured under, migrations, anything now required of the caller.
6. **What is not covered** — known gaps, follow-up work, cases left untested.

Use short paragraphs. Use bullet lists when a change genuinely has several
independent parts; do not turn a single coherent change into a list of files.

Never pad. If a change really is one line with one reason, a subject and a
two-sentence body is the honest length. Length is a consequence of the change
being interesting, not a target.

## Accuracy

- Describe only what is in the staged diff. Do not describe intentions, adjacent
  work, or anything you have not read.
- Do not claim a fix is verified unless the diff contains the test that verifies
  it. If it was checked by hand, say so and say how.
- If the change is a partial fix or a workaround, say that plainly in the body.
  A message that oversells a change is worse than no message.
- Quote real numbers when they are the reason for the change (timings, sizes,
  frame counts) and state what they were measured on.

## This project in particular

- **British spelling** throughout, matching the source comments.
- **Every commit carries a version bump** in `package.json`. That is routine
  bookkeeping: mention the new version once if it is worth knowing, and never
  let it become the subject. A commit whose message is "Bump version" has failed
  to say what the commit was actually for.
- **`src/engine/` must not import a browser API.** That is what lets
  `pnpm verify:pipeline` run the shipping modules under `onnxruntime-node`. A
  commit that moves code between `src/engine/` and `src/worker/` must say which
  direction and why, because the boundary is what keeps the pipeline testable
  rather than an arbitrary bit of file organisation.
- **Inference is serialised deliberately.** `Serializer` in
  `src/engine/runtime.ts` exists because ONNX Runtime Web's WebGPU backend
  shares a command encoder across sessions and concurrent runs there produce
  wrong or failed frames rather than failing cleanly. A commit touching the
  queue must say why the change is safe; "this looked like free parallelism" is
  the mistake the queue is there to prevent.
- The pipeline's numerical constants — warp templates, normalisation means, the
  emap projection, mask feathering — are checked by `verify:pipeline` against
  values captured from the reference pipeline and the macOS app's own output. If
  a commit moves any of them, the body must say what the new reference value is
  and where it came from, and confirm `verify:pipeline` was run.
- Performance claims belong in the body with their conditions: browser and
  version, execution backend (WebGPU or WASM), resolution, whether the enhancer
  was on. A number without those is not a measurement.
- Note when a change is a deliberate divergence from the macOS or iOS app, and
  why. The three are meant to behave the same; an unexplained divergence reads
  as a bug to whoever finds it next.
- `FaceFusion` in comments and asset notes usually means the upstream
  open-source project the pipeline derives from, not this app. Do not describe a
  commit as renaming something when it only touched a citation of that project.
